primitives.name: Signal Detection Probability
primitives.verbatim_quote: Equations & assumptions Likelihood ratio LR = P(observed signal sequence | cheating model with signal probability p) / P(same sequence | honest base-rate model).

primitives.assumptions: Known or estimated p; all trials are independent; signal detection follows Bernoulli process.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If p is misestimated or varies across time, LR becomes misleading; also sensitive to small sample sizes.

layer2.telemetry: Computed likelihood ratio based on observed vs expected signal frequencies.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that alleged cheating can be modeled as a sequence of Bernoulli trials, where each trial represents a potential signal event. Under the honest hypothesis (H0), these events occur at base-rate chance (e.g., 0.5). Under the cheating hypothesis (H1), they occur with a higher probability p. The likelihood ratio (LR) compares how probable the observed sequence is under each model. For instance, in the Astros case, n=267 trials, m=201 eligible for signal detection, b=85 observed signals, and p=0.8. The LR is computed as the product of Bernoulli probabilities under H1 divided by those under H0. This yields an extremely large LR (~3.4×10^30), indicating overwhelming support for the cheating hypothesis. However, this approach assumes independence, known p, and no multiple comparisons. Failure modes include dependence between trials, incorrect estimation of p, and retrospective selection bias. These limitations must be accounted for when applying the framework to real-world scenarios such as GSE’s integrity monitoring.
